items.stem: In an online store, one order can contain many products, and one product appears in many orders. What type of relationship is this?

options.feedback: Correct. Each side can pair with many rows on the other side, so the database needs a third table with one row for each order and product pairing.

options.text: One-to-many, because one order holds many products.
options.feedback: This is true from the order's side only. The same question asked from the product's side also gives many, so the relationship is many-to-many.

options.text: One-to-one, because each line of an order is one product.
options.feedback: A line of an order pairs one order with one product, but the relationship between the two entities is still many on both sides.

options.text: It depends on the database software.
options.feedback: Cardinality comes from the business rules, not from the software. Here the rules allow many on both sides.

items.stem: One course has many sections, and each section belongs to one course. In which table does the foreign key go?

options.text: In the sections table, as a column holding the course id.
options.feedback: Correct. The foreign key goes on the many side, so each section stores the id of its one course.

options.text: In the courses table, as a column holding the section ids.
options.feedback: A column cannot hold a list of ids. The course would need a different number of columns for each course.

options.text: In both tables, so each can find the other.
options.feedback: One foreign key is enough. Storing the link twice lets the two copies disagree.

options.text: In a third table that links courses and sections.
options.feedback: A third table is needed only for many-to-many relationships. A one-to-many relationship needs only the foreign key.

items.stem: A student takes many courses, and a course has many students. A grade is recorded for each student in each course. Where should the grade be stored?

options.text: In the enrollments table, in the row for that student and that course.
options.feedback: Correct. The grade describes the pairing, so it lives in the table that has one row for each pairing.

options.text: In the students table, in a column called grade.
options.feedback: A student has many courses and so would need many grades. One column cannot hold them.

options.text: In the courses table, in a column called grade.
options.feedback: A course has many students, each with a different grade. One column cannot hold them.

options.text: In both the students table and the courses table.
options.feedback: Storing it in both places gives two copies that can disagree, and neither one says which pairing the grade belongs to.
